analysis.one_liner: Strips OSHA of its power to inspect workplaces, cite violators, and impose penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill repealing OSHA's inspection, citation, and penalty authorities never left its House subcommittee and received no vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the sections of the 1970 OSHA law that let the federal government inspect workplaces, investigate records, issue citations, and impose civil and criminal penalties on employers who endanger workers. It would have replaced hard enforcement with cost-benefit tests for new safety standards, a small-business assistance and training program funded by at least a quarter of OSHA's budget, and an awards program for safe companies. It also would have declared that employer-employee safety committees do not count as 'labor organizations' under federal labor law.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those with unsafe workplaces, gain the most: with inspections, citations, and penalties repealed, federal enforcement of workplace safety would essentially end, and the threat of fines for violations would disappear. Small businesses gain targeted consultative services and training. Employers who want to run employee safety committees gain legal clarity that such committees cannot be treated as company unions under the National Labor Relations Act.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the OSHA Act provisions for inspections, investigations, recordkeeping, citations, enforcement procedures, judicial review, and civil and criminal penalties, ending federal enforcement of workplace safety standards.

Requires new OSHA standards to show a reasonable relationship between costs and benefits and to protect workers 'in the most cost-effective manner,' and directs the Secretary to consider costs and feasibility.

Creates a small business assistance and training program with technical and consultative services targeted at small employers and the most hazardous industries, funded by at least one-fourth of OSHA's annual appropriation.

Declares that employee participation committees dealing with workplace safety do not constitute 'labor organizations' under the National Labor Relations Act or representatives under the Railway Labor Act.
Requires the Secretary of Labor to make periodic awards to companies with particularly effective safety programs, which they may use in advertising.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in dangerous industries would bear the cost: with citations, penalties, and enforcement procedures repealed, no federal inspector could compel an employer to fix a hazard, and no fine or criminal charge would follow a violation. Compliance would depend on voluntary programs and assistance. Workers would also have a harder time challenging standards or enforcement in court, since judicial review provisions would be repealed.

drawbacks.text: Repealing citations, penalties, and enforcement procedures would leave no federal mechanism to compel an employer to correct a hazard, making compliance voluntary for employers who chose not to participate in assistance programs.

Requiring each standard to show a reasonable cost-benefit relationship and 'the most cost-effective manner' of protection could delay or block rules on toxic materials and dangerous machinery, since costs to industry would have to be weighed against every safety gain.

Mandating that at least one-fourth of OSHA's appropriation go to assistance and training would shift a quarter of the agency's budget away from enforcement toward services employers may or may not use.

Legalizing employer-run safety committees without union oversight raises the risk that such committees could substitute for genuine worker representation, which is why the National Labor Relations Act has long treated employer-dominated committees as suspect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes a few genuinely useful ideas — consultative help for small businesses, recognition for safe companies, clearer legal ground for safety committees — with a wholesale repeal of OSHA's enforcement power. Because inspections, citations, and penalties are what make safety standards binding, repealing them would leave the entire regulatory structure toothless, and the assistance programs could not force a noncompliant employer to do anything. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the enforcement repeal, not the assistance programs, is the bill's central effect, and that workers in hazardous jobs would bear the risk of voluntary compliance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Joel Hefley introduced the OSHA Reform Act of 1997 on March 20, 1997, joined by 17 Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction.
On April 21, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was recorded.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill never reported out of committee and never receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers are better off in the narrow sense that federal workplace inspections, citations, and penalties remained on the books; employers who would have shed enforcement costs and penalty exposure did not get that relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept OSHA inspections and penalties

for.name: Rep. Joel Hefley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call reveals whether broader support or opposition split by party.

industries.note: The bill repeals OSHA's inspection, citation, and penalty provisions, so employers would no longer face federal enforcement of workplace safety rules. That saving comes at the direct expense of workers' protection on the job.

A new assistance and training program, funded by at least a quarter of OSHA's budget, would provide small employers with consultative services and compliance help targeted at them and the most hazardous industries. Unlike the enforcement repeal, this benefit largely runs alongside workers' interests.

Declaring employer-employee safety committees to be 'labor organizations'-free under the NLRA could let company-run committees substitute for union representation on safety issues. Unions' interest here runs alongside workers' interest in genuine representation.
